summary:
Puducherry is a union territory of India with a partial legislature. Legal recognition of gender identity, identity-document rules and welfare policy for transgender people are set principally by the central government, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file. The framework that reaches a visitor in Puducherry is therefore the national one.

That framework changed in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which amends the 2019 law by removing the right to self-identification, narrowing the definition of transgender person, and limiting legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Human Rights Watch describes the bill as a major reversal of the rights affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling and urged the president not to sign it; both houses had approved the bill and it was awaiting presidential assent at the time of reporting. The amendment mandates medical certification for identity recognition, a direct documents consequence for a trans traveller whose papers now rest on that certification.

Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the accepted categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The government presents the narrower definition as improving delivery of welfare schemes; critics, among them rights activists, warn that it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people, and describe the medical-certification mandate as an attack on privacy and dignity. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
Two readings of the March 2026 amendment compete in the sources. The government argues that a narrower definition improves the targeting and delivery of welfare schemes and widens access to protection from trafficking. Human Rights Watch and rights campaigners, including Akkai Padmashali, describe the same amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist, and as excluding the majority of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal recognition.

Assessments of police conduct diverge in tone rather than in fact. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while the checkpoint incidents on file involve federal security formations rather than ordinary patrol policing: the Railway Protection Force at stations and in custody, and the Central Industrial Security Force at airport screening.

Puducherry sits close to Chennai, where the November 2024 airport stop of Sakshi Jain occurred, so the documented airport-friction pattern is geographically adjacent to the territory even though no Puducherry incident is on file.
localsOnly:
Residents of Puducherry are governed by the same narrowed recognition scheme as visitors: legal recognition of gender identity is limited to historically accepted communities and intersex people, and identity documents for residents now rest on medical certification rather than self-declaration.

The welfare case is the resident-facing stake in the March 2026 amendment. The government's stated purpose is to improve delivery of welfare schemes to eligible beneficiaries under the narrower definition; residents who self-identify as trans men, trans women, non-binary or gender-fluid outside the accepted categories are the people the critics say will lose access to those schemes and to legal protection.

Police treatment of residents is addressed by the Madras High Court's S. Sushma guidelines of 7 June 2021, which bind police on sensitisation, prohibit conversion therapy, and direct the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Residents also live under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in force since 2024, which dropped the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that the Indian Penal Code had provided.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement record, incident series or territorial welfare scheme for trans people is on file; the territory's position in this dossier rests on the national framework and on incidents recorded elsewhere in India.

Whether the president signed the March 2026 amendment is unresolved in the sources, which record the bill as approved by both houses and awaiting assent, with Human Rights Watch urging that it not be signed. The operative date on which medical certification begins to apply to new and existing identity documents is likewise not sourced here.

Whether Puducherry's own administration operates trans-specific welfare schemes, and which high court exercises jurisdiction over the territory, are not sourced in this inventory and remain unresolved.
